explanation: Overstated reach. entriesSeen is declared once per IsPolicySupported call (line 398) and an entry is never removed after it finishes, so the rule is not about a definition 'met again while it is being evaluated' (a true cycle on the current path). Any definition reached a second time anywhere in the evaluation, including a shared, non-circular sub-definition referenced from two places, returns not met. For an All-of definition this changes the outcome: a shared sub-definition that was met the first time counts as not met the second time, so the whole All-of fails. State the rule as 'a definition already visited earlier in the same check counts as not met, even if it was met then or is not part of a cycle'.

Short of its reach. The words 'unless the entry is a version range' imply a plain (non-range) entry for a product is met only when the computer lists that product. Line 385 returns True for that case, but when the product is not listed and has sub-products, a plain entry falls through to the range logic (lines 387-396) with minimum 0 and maximum the highest known version, so a plain entry for a parent product is also met when any of its sub-products (or their children) is installed. Write both outcomes: plain entry met by the product itself or, for a parent product, by any sub-product; range entry met only by sub-products in the version span (and not by the parent itself being listed).

Words are the code's, not the business's: 'when the caller asks for the any-logic option' is the AlwaysUseAny parameter and reads as the opposite of its effect. Say plainly that All-of definitions are only evaluated as All-of when the caller opts in; otherwise every definition is treated as any-one-of. Also state the edge outcomes the lines decide: an All-of definition with no entries is met, an any-of definition with no entries is not met (line 421 returns requireAll).

A clause is false: 'With no list supplied, the key is left cleared' holds only when the element does not keep others. Line 330 clears only if NoPurgeOthers is false, then line 331 skips the rest; with keep-others set and no list supplied, the key is left untouched. Make the no-list outcome follow the keep-others condition.

Two unrelated decisions merged into one: the drop-down choice (the chosen item's value and its value list are written, lines 347-351) and the multi-line text element (saved as multi-string, lines 352-353). Split them into separate rules so each is checkable.

The key-resolution and 'delete / numeric / text' value-writing logic is stated as an Enabled-policy rule, but the same helpers (setValue, setSingleList, setList) decide it for the Disabled policy off-values, checkbox on/off lists and drop-down item lists. Item key: item's own key, else the list's default key, else the element's key (not always the policy's key; for elements the fallback is the element key, lines 303 and 323/351). Either widen this rule's reach to every on/off value and value list, or state the key fallback and the delete/number/text kinds in the rules that use them.

Conflicts with the sibling rule on queued deletion. After a key is cleared, line 188 leaves a '**delvals.' marker, and WillDeleteValue (lines 124-125) then reports every value in that key as queued for deletion, so a value reads as Queued for deletion, not Not configured, until a real value is set. Only the stored record of the value is gone. Decide which state the lifecycle should show and say both facts: the value's own records are forgotten, and the key's clearing marker makes it count as queued for deletion.

A mechanism (the type guard in an equality override), not a business decision; it costs the reader's trust. Drop it. The case-insensitive pair matching is already stated by the sibling rule and by the case-insensitivity rules for POL and REG files.

A build-time mechanism (generating a source file from git), not a rule the product decides about policies; the version label is not decided for or by any capability's business data. Drop it, or if kept record it as an assumption about build, not a rule.

A parsing mechanism (null-safe attribute read), not a business rule, and it is subsumed by the next rule on defaults. Drop it. Keep the default-on-missing-or-invalid rule, which does change how malformed definition files behave.

Missing a consequence the lines decide: applying a 'Not Configured' (or any state) first forgets the policy (line 212), and SetPolicyState writes nothing for Not Configured, so Not Configured is achieved purely by the forget step. Also an unknown policy ID fails at line 210 before the comment is saved or anything is forgotten, while a failure inside SetPolicyState after the forget leaves the policy forgotten (state lost). Say these, and that an empty comment in the script does not erase an existing comment.

says: SetPolicyState decides nothing for Not Configured or Unknown: its Select Case (PolicyProcessing.vb 297-378) has only Enabled and Disabled branches, so it writes nothing for the other states. Whoever calls it must forget the policy's values first (SpolFile.vb 212 does). A reader rebuilding 'Setting policies' needs this stated as a rule of the block: the Not Configured state is not written by this routine, it is the absence of values produced by the forget step; and Enabled/Disabled writes do not themselves remove stale values left by a previous state (only elements' own deletes/clears do).

A REG file is only a write target: GetValue, ContainsValue, WillDeleteValue, GetValueNames and ForgetValue throw 'not implemented' (RegFile.vb 214-225, 237-239) and the file says it is not a valid policy source for any policy loader (lines 4-5). The consequence that changes a decision: exporting changes into a REG file works for set, delete and clear, but a difference-apply that has to forget values (PolFile.ApplyDifference, PolicySource.vb 174-177, which calls ForgetValue on the target) fails if it targets a REG file, and a REG file cannot be read back as a policy source. Write it as a rule of the REG block, naming which operations it supports.

A SPOL script is refused as a whole, with the line number, for structural faults the option parser does not tolerate: an option line without ': ' (SpolFile.vb 90-91), a repeated option name within one policy (line 121, Dictionary.Add), a '[' block never closed with ']' (107-109), a list entry with no quoted text (113-116), and a policy header or state line missing at the end of the text (53-54, 57, 78). None of these is stated; the state-and-option rules read as if only the listed messages exist. Add rules (or one per distinct refusal) so a rebuild keeps them.
